gloss: The smaller of the two houses of a national or state legislature.
examples: The bill passed the *senate* by a single vote.
She served four years in the state *senate*.
Several state *senates* have taken up the same question.

gloss: A member of a senate.
examples: Our *senator* voted against the bill.
He was first elected *senator* twelve years ago.
Both *senators* from our state showed up to the hearing.

gloss: The national lawmaking body of a country, especially the House and Senate in the United States.
examples: *Congress* has to approve the money before anything gets built.
The president asked *Congress* for emergency funding.
She has worked in *Congress* since she was twenty-five.

gloss: A person elected to speak and vote for a group of citizens.
examples: Call your *representative* and tell her how you feel about it.
He is the *representative* for our district.
Two hundred *representatives* signed the letter.

gloss: The body of elected people that makes the laws of a state or country.
examples: The *legislature* meets for ninety days every year.
It took the state *legislature* three sessions to pass it.
Most state *legislatures* are back in session in January.

gloss: Laws considered together, or the making of laws.
examples: New *legislation* on health insurance takes effect in July.
The governor is pushing for *legislation* to fix the roads.
There is very little *legislation* on this yet.
contrast: Uncountable: say a piece of legislation or a bill, never a legislation.

gloss: An elected official whose job is to write and pass laws.
examples: One *lawmaker* walked out in the middle of the vote.
*Lawmakers* have until Friday to reach a deal.
The *lawmakers* who wrote the bill defended it on television.

gloss: A group of people who meet officially to make decisions or laws.
examples: The state *assembly* voted to raise the minimum wage.
She spoke in front of the general *assembly*.
Both *assemblies* rejected the plan.

gloss: A group elected or chosen to run a town, organization, or program.
examples: The city *council* meets on the first Tuesday of the month.
Our *council* voted to close the street to cars.
Neighborhood *councils* have almost no real power here.
contrast: Sounds exactly like counsel (advice, or a lawyer); the group is spelled council.

gloss: A department of government that handles one area of public business.
examples: A federal *agency* is looking into the spill.
The *agency* has about two thousand employees.
Three *agencies* are fighting over the same budget.

gloss: The people who run a government during one leader's time in office.
examples: The current *administration* has cut taxes twice.
That rule was written under the previous *administration*.
Both *administrations* handled the border the same way.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: The legal right to give orders, or a public body that has that right.
examples: The mayor has no *authority* over the school district.
The port *authority* owns all three bridges.
Local *authorities* closed the road for two days.
contrast: Uncountable when it means power; countable when it means an official body.

gloss: A government department in charge of one area, such as defense or health.
examples: The foreign *ministry* issued a statement.
She spent ten years at the *ministry* of education.
Two *ministries* were merged to save money.
contrast: The US has no ministries; the same bodies are called departments.

gloss: A senior member of a government who is in charge of a department.
examples: The finance *minister* resigned over the scandal.
He met with the defense *minister* in Berlin.
Several *ministers* were replaced last month.
contrast: In the US the same job title is secretary, not minister.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: Complicated official rules and paperwork, or the body of officials who apply them.
examples: Getting a permit here means months of *bureaucracy*.
The federal *bureaucracy* employs millions of people.
Big *bureaucracies* are slow to change.

gloss: The office in a foreign capital where a country's ambassador works.
examples: You can apply for the visa at the *embassy*.
The American *embassy* is two blocks from the park.
Several *embassies* closed for the holiday.

gloss: A smaller foreign government office that helps its citizens and issues visas.
examples: The nearest *consulate* is in Chicago.
She picked up her passport at the *consulate*.
They have *consulates* in six American cities.

gloss: The place or body that decides legal cases and settles disputes.
examples: The case goes to *court* in March.
A federal *court* blocked the new rule.
Lower *courts* had already ruled the other way.

gloss: The building where a legislature meets.
examples: Protesters gathered on the steps of the *capitol*.
The state *capitol* is open to visitors on weekdays.
Many state *capitols* were built in the same style.
contrast: Sounds exactly like capital; the building ends in -ol, the city and the money in -al.

gloss: The building that holds a city's government offices.
examples: You can pay the ticket at *city hall*.
The rally started in front of *city hall*.
Both *city halls* were built in the 1920s.

gloss: A local division of a state, with its own courts, sheriff, and officials.
examples: Our *county* runs the library system.
He was born in the next *county* over.
All five *counties* voted the same way.

gloss: An area marked out for voting, schools, or local administration.
examples: She represents the third *district*.
The school *district* is closing two buildings.
The map redrew half the *districts* in the state.

gloss: A small area used for voting or policing.
examples: Turnout was heavy in our *precinct*.
They took him down to the *precinct* for questioning.
Results from twelve *precincts* are still missing.

gloss: One of the regions with its own government that make up the US, or a country as a political body.
examples: Each *state* writes its own election rules.
The *state* pays for most of the highway work.
Twelve *states* joined the lawsuit.

gloss: A country and the people who belong to it.
examples: The whole *nation* watched the speech.
He called it the richest *nation* on earth.
Forty *nations* signed the agreement.

gloss: A country whose head of state is elected rather than born into the job.
examples: The country became a *republic* in 1918.
It is a *republic* in name only.
Several former *republics* still use the old currency.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: Government by the people through free elections, or a country run that way.
examples: *Democracy* only works if people show up to vote.
The country is now a stable *democracy*.
Western *democracies* reacted the same way.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: Rule by a king or queen, or a country governed that way.
examples: The country has been a *monarchy* for six hundred years.
*Monarchy* still has strong support there.
Most European *monarchies* have no real power now.
contrast: The ch is a k sound: MAH-nur-kee.

gloss: A king or queen who is the head of a state.
examples: The *monarch* signs the law but never writes it.
She is the longest-serving *monarch* in their history.
European *monarchs* met at the funeral.
contrast: The ch is a k sound; the same word also names an orange and black butterfly.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: Government by one person or group with total power, or a country run that way.
examples: The island lived under a *dictatorship* for thirty years.

Both *dictatorships* collapsed within months of each other.

gloss: A ruler with complete power who was not freely elected.
examples: The *dictator* fled the country overnight.
He governs like a *dictator*.
Two *dictators* were driven out that same year.
contrast: Americans stress the first syllable, DIK-tay-tur; the British say dik-TAY-tuh.

gloss: A government in power, especially one seen as harsh or undemocratic.
examples: The old *regime* jailed anyone who spoke up.
Sanctions were aimed at the *regime*, not the people.
Two *regimes* fell in the same decade.
contrast: The g is the zh sound in measure, not a hard g.

gloss: A group of countries or peoples ruled by one government or emperor.
examples: The *empire* stretched across three continents.
The war brought down the *empire*.
All the old *empires* are gone now.

gloss: The elected head of state in a republic.
examples: The *president* signed the bill on Tuesday.
She is running for *president* next year.
Four *presidents* attended the funeral.
contrast: Do not confuse it with precedent (PRESS-uh-duhnt), an earlier case used as an example.

gloss: The official who ranks just below the president and takes over if needed.
examples: The *vice president* broke the tie in the Senate.
He picked a governor as his *vice president*.
Two former *vice presidents* were in the room.
contrast: Americans usually write it without a hyphen; elsewhere it is often vice-president.

gloss: The head of government in a country that has a parliament.
examples: The *prime minister* called an early election.
She met the *prime minister* in London.
Three *prime ministers* came and went in one year.

gloss: The elected head of a US state government.
examples: The *governor* declared a state of emergency.
He was *governor* for two terms.
Ten *governors* signed the joint letter.
contrast: The first o sounds like uh: GUV-ur-nur, not GOV-.

gloss: The elected head of a city or town government.
examples: The *mayor* wants to hire two hundred more officers.

Big-city *mayors* met in Washington last week.
contrast: Americans say it in two syllables, MAY-ur; the British make it rhyme with air.

gloss: Someone who holds or is running for elected office.
examples: No *politician* wants to talk about raising taxes.
He was a career *politician* for forty years.
Voters here do not trust *politicians* much.

gloss: An official who represents his or her country in another country.
examples: A senior *diplomat* was sent to the talks.
Her father was a *diplomat*, so she grew up abroad.
Six *diplomats* were expelled last month.

gloss: The top official who represents one country in another.
examples: The *ambassador* was called home for consultations.
He served as *ambassador* to Japan.
Both *ambassadors* skipped the ceremony.

gloss: A person who holds a position of authority in a government or organization.
examples: A city *official* confirmed the closure.
The *official* refused to give her name.
Health *officials* are urging people to stay home.

gloss: A person who is second in rank and acts for the person above them.
examples: His *deputy* ran the office while he was away.
She was named *deputy* director in the spring.
Two *deputies* handled the paperwork.
contrast: A false friend: an elected member of parliament is a representative, not a deputy.

gloss: An assistant who works closely with an important official.
examples: A senior *aide* leaked the memo.
His *aide* handed him a note in the middle of the speech.
Two *aides* resigned the same week.
contrast: Sounds exactly like aid (help); the person is spelled with an e on the end.

gloss: Someone whose job is to give official advice to a leader.
examples: He is the president's chief economic *adviser*.
Her *adviser* told her not to run.
The *advisers* disagreed with each other in public.
contrast: Advisor is an equally correct American spelling.

gloss: A person chosen to speak publicly for an organization or official.
examples: A *spokesperson* for the agency denied the report.
The company *spokesperson* would not take questions.
*Spokespeople* for both campaigns gave the same answer.
contrast: The plural is usually spokespeople, though spokespersons is also used.

gloss: Someone paid to persuade lawmakers to vote a certain way.
examples: A *lobbyist* for the drug industry wrote most of that language.
He quit the Senate and became a *lobbyist*.
*Lobbyists* filled the hallway outside the hearing.

gloss: Someone who works actively for political or social change.
examples: She has been a housing *activist* since college.
One *activist* chained herself to the fence.
*Activists* have been camped outside all week.

gloss: A person taking part in a public demonstration against something.

One *protester* held a sign the whole time.
*Protesters* blocked traffic on the bridge.
contrast: Stress falls on the second syllable here, unlike the noun protest (PROH-test).

gloss: An official in a large government department, especially one who follows rules rigidly.
examples: Some *bureaucrat* in the capital decided it for us.
He is a career *bureaucrat* with thirty years in.
*Bureaucrats* wrote the rule, not elected officials.

gloss: A person sent to a meeting or convention to represent others.
examples: Each *delegate* gets one vote on the floor.
She went as a *delegate* from our county.
He needs two thousand *delegates* to win the nomination.
contrast: The noun ends in -guht; the verb delegate ends in -gayt.

gloss: The person a party or leader has officially chosen for an office or award.
examples: She became the party's *nominee* in July.
The *nominee* still has to be confirmed by the Senate.
Both *nominees* refused to debate.

gloss: The person currently holding an elected office.
examples: The *incumbent* usually has a big advantage.
She is running against a three-term *incumbent*.
Most *incumbents* were reelected easily.

gloss: A person who has the right to vote, or who votes in an election.
examples: Every registered *voter* got a ballot in the mail.
The average *voter* here is over fifty.
*Voters* rejected the tax increase.

gloss: A person who pays taxes to the government.
examples: The bailout cost the *taxpayer* billions.
As a *taxpayer*, I want to know where the money went.
*Taxpayers* are still paying for that stadium.

gloss: Someone who has served in the armed forces.
examples: My grandfather is a *veteran* of the Korean War.
The clinic treats only *veterans*.
*Veterans* march downtown every November.
contrast: Often shortened in speech to two syllables, VET-ruhn.

gloss: A person employed by the government who is not an elected official.
examples: She spent her whole career as a *civil servant*.
A *civil servant* keeps working when the government changes.
Thousands of *civil servants* went without pay.

gloss: An insider who reports illegal or dishonest conduct inside an organization.
examples: A *whistleblower* handed the documents to a reporter.
The law protects any *whistleblower* who comes forward.
Two *whistleblowers* testified behind closed doors.
contrast: The t in whistle is silent: WISS-uhl.

gloss: The person who takes over a job or position from someone else.
examples: He named his own *successor* before leaving.
Her *successor* reversed almost every decision.
Both of his *successors* kept the policy.

gloss: An organized event in which people vote to choose officials.
examples: The *election* is the first Tuesday in November.
He lost the *election* by four hundred votes.
Local *elections* draw very few voters.
contrast: English uses the singular for one event: an election, where Russian says выборы.

gloss: The paper or screen on which a voter marks a choice.
examples: My name was not on the *ballot*.
She filled out her *ballot* at the kitchen table.
They are still counting mail-in *ballots*.

gloss: A formal choice made in an election or a meeting.
examples: The measure passed by one *vote*.
The Senate holds a *vote* on Thursday.
She got more *votes* than the other two combined.

gloss: The number of people who actually vote or show up.
examples: *Turnout* was under thirty percent.
They expect record *turnout* this year.
*Turnouts* like that are rare in a primary.

gloss: A survey of people's opinions, or the place where votes are cast.
examples: A new *poll* puts her six points ahead.
The *polls* close at eight.
Recent *polls* have all said the same thing.
contrast: Sounds exactly like pole (a long stick).

gloss: An organized effort to win an election or achieve a public goal.
examples: Her *campaign* raised two million dollars.
He ran a quiet *campaign* and still won.
Both *campaigns* went negative in the last week.
contrast: The g is silent: kam-PAYN.

gloss: The act of officially proposing someone for an office or honor.
examples: She won the *nomination* on the first ballot.
His *nomination* went to the Senate in June.
Three *nominations* are still waiting for a vote.

gloss: An election in which a party's voters choose its candidate for the main election.
examples: He lost the *primary* but stayed in politics.
The *primary* is in March this year.
She campaigned in a dozen *primaries*.

gloss: A meeting of party members to pick candidates or agree on policy.
examples: The *caucus* met for two hours behind closed doors.
He came in second in the Iowa *caucus*.
Both *caucuses* endorsed the same bill.

gloss: A second election held between the top two candidates when no one wins outright.
examples: Nobody got fifty percent, so there will be a *runoff*.
She won the *runoff* easily.
Two *runoffs* are scheduled for December.

gloss: The fixed period a person serves in an elected office.
examples: A senator's *term* is six years.
He is in his second *term* as mayor.
Some states limit governors to two *terms*.

gloss: The authority a government claims from voters, or an official order to do something.
examples: He says the win gives him a *mandate* to raise taxes.
The city dropped the mask *mandate* in April.
Several *mandates* were struck down in court.

gloss: The set of positions a party or candidate runs on.
examples: Health care is the center of her *platform*.
The party adopted its *platform* at the convention.
Their two *platforms* are almost identical.

gloss: A public statement of support for a candidate or proposal.
examples: The union's *endorsement* was worth a lot in that district.
He picked up the *endorsement* of the local paper.
She has more *endorsements* than anyone in the race.

gloss: A short phrase used to sum up a campaign or cause.
examples: Their *slogan* was on every yard sign in town.
It was a catchy *slogan* with nothing behind it.
The crowd chanted the same two *slogans* all afternoon.

gloss: A formal public discussion in which opposing sides argue their case.
examples: The first *debate* is next Wednesday night.
He skipped the *debate* and held a rally instead.
Both *debates* were watched by millions.

gloss: A large public meeting held to support a cause or candidate.
examples: The *rally* drew about five thousand people.
She spoke at a *rally* outside the capitol.
He held three *rallies* in two days.

gloss: A large official meeting of a party or organization.
examples: The party *convention* runs for four days.
She accepted the nomination at the *convention*.
Both *conventions* are held in the summer.

gloss: All the people entitled to vote in an election.
examples: The *electorate* here is older than the national average.
He misread the mood of the *electorate*.
The two *electorates* look nothing alike.

gloss: The basic set of laws that says how a country is governed.
examples: The *constitution* guarantees a jury trial.
That law was found to violate the state *constitution*.
Most state *constitutions* are far longer than the federal one.
contrast: Americans say -TOO-shuhn; the British say -TYOO-shuhn.

gloss: A formal change or addition made to a law or constitution.
examples: The First *Amendment* protects free speech.
His *amendment* failed by two votes.
They attached six *amendments* to the bill.

gloss: A written law passed by a legislature.
examples: The *statute* has been on the books since 1974.
No federal *statute* covers this situation.
Several old *statutes* were finally repealed.
contrast: Say STACH-oot, and do not mix it up with statue (a sculpture).

gloss: A law passed by a city or county government.
examples: A city *ordinance* bans fireworks inside town limits.
The council passed the *ordinance* unanimously.
Noise *ordinances* differ from town to town.

gloss: A formal written agreement between countries.
examples: The *treaty* took four years to negotiate.

gloss: A change made to improve a system, law, or institution.
examples: Immigration *reform* has stalled again.
The *reform* passed with support from both parties.
These *reforms* will take years to show results.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: An official rule made by a government agency, or the act of controlling something by rules.
examples: A new *regulation* limits how much they can charge.
The industry has almost no *regulation*.
Safety *regulations* were tightened after the fire.

gloss: Government money and services given to people in need.
examples: She was on *welfare* for about a year.
The state cut *welfare* spending again.
*Welfare* rules changed a lot in the nineties.
contrast: Uncountable: never a welfare or welfares.

gloss: Money paid by a government to help an industry or keep prices low.
examples: The farm *subsidy* has been in place for decades.
Without the *subsidy*, the fare would double.
Congress voted to end several *subsidies*.

gloss: The system of medical services a country provides to its people.
examples: *Healthcare* was the top issue in the election.
Millions of people still have no *healthcare*.
They promised cheaper *healthcare* for everyone.
contrast: Also written as two words, health care; both are common in the US.

gloss: The movement of people into a country to live there.
examples: *Immigration* dominated the debate.

The *immigration* system has not been updated in years.
contrast: Immigration is movement into a country; emigration is movement out of one.

gloss: An official penalty, usually trade or financial, imposed on a country.
examples: A new *sanction* targets the country's banks.
The *sanctions* took effect at midnight.
They lifted the *sanctions* after the election.

gloss: Close watching of people or places by police or government.
examples: The house was under *surveillance* for a month.
New *surveillance* cameras went up downtown.
The bill would expand government *surveillance*.
contrast: No y sound in the middle: sur-VAY-luhns.

gloss: The roads, bridges, water lines, and other basic systems a country runs on.
examples: The bill puts a trillion dollars into *infrastructure*.
Our *infrastructure* is falling apart.
*Infrastructure* spending creates a lot of jobs.

gloss: The system by which a government collects taxes.
examples: The colonists objected to *taxation* without representation.
*Taxation* here falls hardest on the middle class.
He wants to shift *taxation* from income to spending.

gloss: The government department that manages public money.
examples: The *Treasury* borrowed another two hundred billion.
That money comes straight out of the state *treasury*.
Finance ministers run their national *treasuries*.

gloss: Money provided for a program or organization.
examples: Federal *funding* pays for most of the research.
The school lost its *funding* last year.
They are asking Congress for more *funding*.
contrast: Uncountable: say more funding, never more fundings.

gloss: An official document that allows you to do something.
examples: You need a *permit* to hold a march downtown.
The building *permit* took three months.
The city issued two hundred *permits* last year.
contrast: The noun is PUR-mit; the verb permit is pur-MIT.

gloss: Official permission, in document form, to do or own something.
examples: Bring your driver's *license* to the polling place.
The bar lost its liquor *license*.
The state issues about a million *licenses* a year.
contrast: Americans spell both the noun and the verb license; the British write licence for the noun.

gloss: The act of putting your name on an official list.
examples: Voter *registration* closes two weeks before the election.
*Registration* is free and takes five minutes online.
They ran a *registration* drive at the college.

gloss: An official decision made by a judge or court.
examples: The *ruling* came down on a Friday afternoon.
The state is appealing the *ruling*.
Two earlier *rulings* said the opposite.

gloss: An official meeting at which evidence and arguments are heard.
examples: The committee held a *hearing* on the crash.

The *hearings* went on for three days.

gloss: A legal order requiring someone to appear or hand over documents.
examples: The committee issued a *subpoena* for the emails.
He ignored the *subpoena* and was held in contempt.
Both *subpoenas* were fought in court.
contrast: The b is silent: suh-PEE-nuh.

gloss: A period during which a legislature or court meets and works.
examples: The bill died at the end of the *session*.
The governor called a special *session*.
Two *sessions* passed with no action on it.

gloss: The formal charging of a public official with serious wrongdoing in office.
examples: The House voted for *impeachment* along party lines.
*Impeachment* does not automatically remove someone from office.
There have been only a handful of presidential *impeachments*.

gloss: An official act freeing someone from punishment for a crime.
examples: The governor granted him a full *pardon*.

He issued a hundred *pardons* on his last day.

gloss: A long speech or delay used in the Senate to block a vote.

gloss: A period when a government stops most work because no budget has been approved.
examples: The *shutdown* lasted thirty-five days.

Two *shutdowns* happened in the same year.

gloss: The work of managing relations between countries through talks rather than force.

It took years of *diplomacy* to get the deal.

gloss: A formal agreement between countries or groups to work together.
examples: The *alliance* has thirty member countries.

Old *alliances* are being tested again.

gloss: A temporary union of parties or groups formed for a common purpose.
examples: The two parties formed a *coalition* government.

Both *coalitions* collapsed within a year.

gloss: Formal discussion aimed at reaching an agreement.
examples: The *negotiation* broke down over money.

gloss: A group of people sent to represent a country or organization.
examples: A *delegation* from the state met with the president.

gloss: A country's right to govern itself without outside control.

*Sovereignty* over the islands is still disputed.

gloss: Land under the control of a government.

Puerto Rico is a US *territory*, not a state.
Several overseas *territories* still vote in their elections.

gloss: An agreement to stop fighting, usually for a set time.
examples: The *ceasefire* held for about a week.
Both sides agreed to a temporary *ceasefire*.
Earlier *ceasefires* had broken down within days.

gloss: Official permission stamped in a passport to enter or stay in a country.
examples: Her student *visa* runs out in June.

gloss: The official document that proves your nationality when you travel abroad.

gloss: Protection given by a country to someone fleeing danger at home.

gloss: The legal status of belonging to a particular country.
examples: She got her American *citizenship* last year.

gloss: The country a person legally belongs to.

contrast: In American forms nationality means citizenship, not ethnic background.

gloss: The forced removal of a person from a country.
examples: He is fighting *deportation* in court.

gloss: A country or person that supports another, especially in a conflict.
examples: Canada has been a close *ally* for a century.
He was the president's most reliable *ally* in the Senate.
Our *allies* were told about the strike in advance.
contrast: The noun is stressed on the first syllable, AL-eye; the verb ally is uh-LY.

gloss: Money, food, or supplies given by a government to people or countries in need.
examples: Congress approved another billion dollars in *aid*.
Foreign *aid* is a tiny share of the budget.
*Aid* trucks finally crossed the border.
contrast: Uncountable, and a homophone of aide, which is a person.

gloss: Something a person is legally or morally allowed to have or do.
examples: You have the *right* to remain silent.
Voting is a *right*, not a favor.
The law took away *rights* people had for fifty years.
contrast: Sounds exactly like write and rite.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: Freedom from government control, or a specific freedom guaranteed by law.
examples: They fought for *liberty* and lost everything else.
The case is about religious *liberty*.
Civil *liberties* groups sued the state.

gloss: The state of everyone having the same rights and status.
examples: The movement fought for racial *equality*.
*Equality* before the law is the whole idea.
There is still no *equality* in pay.

gloss: Dishonest use of public office for private gain.
examples: He was convicted of *corruption* in office.
*Corruption* runs through the whole permit system.
Voters were tired of the *corruption* at city hall.

gloss: Money or a gift given illegally to get someone to act in your favor.
examples: He took a *bribe* to approve the permit.
The inspector was offered a *bribe* and reported it.
Prosecutors say the *bribes* went on for years.

gloss: A public event that shocks people because someone acted dishonestly.
examples: The *scandal* ended his career.
A corruption *scandal* brought down the mayor.
Two *scandals* hit the department in one month.

gloss: Information spread to push a political view, often misleading.
examples: State television is pure *propaganda*.
They dismissed the report as *propaganda*.
Wartime *propaganda* posters are on display.

gloss: Official control over what may be published, said, or shown.
examples: The law amounts to *censorship*, the paper said.
*Censorship* of textbooks became a campaign issue.
They accused the platform of *censorship*.
contrast: From censor (an official); do not confuse it with sensor, a device.

gloss: A public demonstration against something people think is wrong.
examples: The *protest* stayed peaceful all afternoon.
A small *protest* formed outside the courthouse.
*Protests* spread to a dozen cities.
contrast: The noun is PROH-test; the verb protest is pruh-TEST.

gloss: A public gathering held to show support for or opposition to something.
examples: The *demonstration* drew ten thousand people.
Police estimated the *demonstration* at half that.
*Demonstrations* went on for three nights.

gloss: Violent disorder by a crowd in a public place.
examples: The arrest touched off a *riot*.
A *riot* broke out after the game.
The *riots* lasted two nights.

gloss: The overthrow of a government by the people, usually by force.
examples: The *revolution* began with a strike at the shipyard.
He wrote a book about the French *revolution*.
Two *revolutions* in one century wore the country out.

gloss: A sudden illegal takeover of a government, usually by the military.
examples: The army seized power in a *coup*.
The *coup* failed within forty-eight hours.
There have been three *coups* since independence.
contrast: The p is silent; it rhymes with too.

gloss: An organized armed or open refusal to obey a government.
examples: The *rebellion* started in the mountains.
Troops put down the *rebellion* in a week.
Earlier *rebellions* had all been crushed.

gloss: A group of people working together for a shared political or social goal.
examples: The labor *movement* built this city.
She joined the *movement* in her twenties.
Both *movements* grew out of the same protests.

gloss: A signed request asking officials to do something.
examples: The *petition* got forty thousand signatures.
Sign the *petition* if you agree.
Two *petitions* were filed with the county clerk.

gloss: The political parties or groups that are against the government in power.
examples: The *opposition* walked out of the vote.
There is strong *opposition* to the plan in rural areas.
Leaders of the *opposition* were arrested.

gloss: The smaller part of a group, or a group that differs from most of the population.
examples: Only a small *minority* voted against it.
His party is in the *minority* this session.
The law was written to protect ethnic *minorities*.

gloss: A system of political ideas that shapes what a group believes and does.
examples: Their *ideology* has not changed in forty years.
He puts *ideology* ahead of results.
The two *ideologies* have almost nothing in common.
contrast: It starts with the sound eye, not ih.

gloss: A person who favors traditional values and limited government.
examples: She is a fiscal *conservative* but not a social one.
Every *conservative* in the room applauded.
*Conservatives* control the state legislature.

gloss: A person who favors social reform and an active role for government.
examples: He was the most outspoken *liberal* in the Senate.
As a *liberal*, she supports higher taxes on the wealthy.
*Liberals* and conservatives agreed on this one bill.
contrast: In American politics liberal means left of center, not free-market as in Europe.

gloss: A system in which the government or the public owns and runs major industries.
examples: Critics called the plan *socialism*.
*Socialism* means different things to different voters.
He campaigned openly on democratic *socialism*.

gloss: A system in which the state owns all property and a single party rules.
examples: *Communism* collapsed across the region in 1991.
Her parents fled *communism* as teenagers.
The party abandoned *communism* in everything but name.

gloss: An economic system in which businesses and property are privately owned.
examples: American *capitalism* has always had rules.
The debate is really about *capitalism* itself.
He defends *capitalism* but wants stronger regulation.

gloss: Strong loyalty to one's own nation, often to the exclusion of others.
examples: *Nationalism* has been rising across Europe.
He ran on economic *nationalism*.
The war was driven by *nationalism* on both sides.

gloss: Love of and pride in one's own country.
examples: He talks about *patriotism* in every speech.
For her, *patriotism* means paying your taxes.
*Patriotism* and nationalism are not the same thing.
contrast: Americans begin it with PAY-, not the British PAT-.

gloss: Freedom from control by another country or authority.
examples: The country won its *independence* in 1960.
The agency guards its *independence* from the White House.
The colonies declared *independence* in 1776.

gloss: Public anger and disorder that threatens stability.
examples: Months of *unrest* followed the election.
There is growing *unrest* in the countryside.
The *unrest* died down once the prices fell.
contrast: Uncountable: never an unrest or unrests.

gloss: Protection of a country or people from attack and danger.
examples: National *security* was the reason they gave.
*Security* at the airport was unusually tight.
The committee meets to discuss border *security*.

gloss: The protection of a country against attack, and the money and forces used for it.
examples: *Defense* takes up a huge share of the budget.
She works at the Department of *Defense*.
They voted to raise *defense* spending again.
contrast: Americans spell it defense; the British write defence.

gloss: A country's armed forces taken as a whole.
examples: He joined the *military* right out of high school.
The *military* stayed out of the dispute.
The *military* is the largest employer in the state.
contrast: Used with the: the military, never a military or militaries.

gloss: Armed fighting between countries or groups.
examples: The *war* lasted four years.
Congress has not declared a *war* since 1942.
Both *wars* started over the same border.

gloss: The use of violence against civilians to achieve political aims.
examples: He was charged with *terrorism*.
The law was written after an act of domestic *terrorism*.
*Terrorism* reshaped how Americans travel.

gloss: A piece of cloth with a design that stands for a country or group.
examples: The *flag* was flying at half-staff.
Every classroom has a *flag* on the wall.
*Flags* lined both sides of the street.

gloss: The official song of a country, played on formal occasions.
examples: Everyone stood for the national *anthem*.
She sang the *anthem* before the game.
Both national *anthems* were played.

gloss: A formal promise, often made publicly before taking office.
examples: She took the *oath* of office at noon.
He swore an *oath* to defend the constitution.
The new officers repeated their *oaths* together.
contrast: The plural oaths is said with a voiced th, like OHTHZ.

gloss: The ceremony at which someone formally takes office.
examples: The *inauguration* is held in January.
It rained through the whole *inauguration*.
The last two *inaugurations* were much smaller.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: A formal talk given to an audience, or the act of speaking freely.
examples: His *speech* lasted forty minutes.
Free *speech* is protected by the First Amendment.
She gave three *speeches* in one day.
contrast: Countable for a talk; uncountable in phrases like freedom of speech.

gloss: Newspapers, television, and other news media taken together.
examples: The *press* was kept outside the building.
He rarely talks to the *press*.
The story got a lot of *press* that week.
contrast: Uncountable and used with the: the press, never a press for the news media.

gloss: A meeting at which an official answers questions from reporters.
examples: The governor called a *press conference* for four o'clock.
She announced it at a *press conference* on the steps.
He held two *press conferences* in one day.
